paragraphs.text: Idiopathic torsion dystonia (ITD) is a movement disorder characterized by sustained muscle contractions that appear as twisting movements of the limbs, trunk, and/or neck and can progress to abnormal postures (Kramer et al., 1990). The DYT1 form typically begins in childhood (Ozelius et al., 9288096 (1997)). In carriers of the Ashkenazi Jewish founder mutation, symptoms usually begin in a limb (Bressman et al., 1994). Inheritance is autosomal dominant with reduced penetrance, estimated at 30 to 40% (Ozelius et al., 9149944 (1997)).

paragraphs.text: Bundey et al. (1975) carried out a family study of 32 patients with torsion dystonia. They concluded that there were at least 2 forms of generalized dystonia with childhood onset, an autosomal dominant form and an autosomal recessive form, and that the 2 forms could not be told apart clinically. Because of a probable paternal age effect, they thought that 9 to 11 patients with generalized childhood dystonia represented new dominant mutations. Fitness with childhood onset was 1/20 of normal. Most of the other 15 patients, 12 of whom had onset in adult life, appeared to have nongenetic torsion dystonia.

paragraphs.text: Bressman et al. (1994) used 9q34 markers (D9S62, D9S63, and ASS) to classify 174 Ashkenazi Jewish individuals with idiopathic torsion dystonia as carriers, noncarriers, or ambiguous with respect to a DYT1-associated haplotype. There were 90 carriers, 70 noncarriers, and 14 ambiguous individuals. Mean age at onset was 12.5 +/- 8.2 years in carriers and 36.5 +/- 16.4 years in noncarriers. In 94% of carriers, symptoms began in a limb, with arm and leg equally affected; onset was rarely in the neck (3.3%) or larynx (2.2%). In noncarriers, the neck, larynx, and other cranial muscles were the site of onset in 79%, the arms in 21%, and the legs never. Limb onset, leg involvement during the course of the disease, and age at onset distinguished carriers from noncarriers with 90% accuracy.

paragraphs.text: Heiman et al. (2004) gave a standardized psychiatric interview to members of families with a DYT1 mutation: 96 manifesting carriers, 60 nonmanifesting carriers, and 65 noncarriers. Compared with noncarriers, the risk of recurrent major depressive disorder was increased in nonmanifesting carriers (RR = 4.95) and in manifesting carriers (RR = 3.62). Carriers also had an earlier age at onset of recurrent major depression. The severity of motor signs was not associated with the likelihood of recurrent depression, and carriers did not have an increased risk of single major depression or bipolar disorder. The authors suggested that early-onset recurrent depression is a clinical expression of the DYT1 mutation.

paragraphs.text: Lorden et al. (1984) described the dystonic (dt) rat, an autosomal recessive mutant of Sprague-Dawley rats. Sustained twisting movements begin on postnatal day 10. The mutants had no morphologic lesions but had significantly raised cerebellar norepinephrine levels and were less sensitive to the akinesic effects of haloperidol.

checks.evidence_quote: An inherited neurological disorder characterized by sustained twisting movements during waking has been discovered in Sprague-Dawley rats. The mutation follows an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance and has been named dystonic (dt).
checks.explanation: The abstract says the dt mutation arose in Sprague-Dawley rats and is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait.

checks.claim: In the dystonic (dt) rat, sustained twisting movements begin on postnatal day 10.

checks.explanation: The abstract gives postnatal day 10 as the onset of clinical signs, and twisting is one of those signs.

checks.claim: The dystonic (dt) rat mutants had no morphologic lesions.
checks.evidence_quote: No morphological lesions of neural or non-neural tissues have been observed with routine light microscopy.

checks.evidence_quote: Dystonic rats demonstrate significantly elevated cerebellar norepinephrine levels

checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

paragraphs.text: Shashidharan et al. (2005) generated 4 transgenic mouse lines overexpressing human deltaE-torsinA from a neuron-specific enolase promoter. As early as 3 weeks after birth, the mice developed dystonic-appearing self-clasping of the limbs, hyperkinesia, and rapid bidirectional circling, with about 40% of mice in each line severely affected. Affected mice had decreased striatal dopamine, whereas unaffected transgenic mice had increased levels. Perinuclear inclusions positive for ubiquitin, torsinA, and lamin were found in the pedunculopontine nucleus and other brainstem regions, a pattern similar to that described in DYT1 patients.

The deletion removes 1 of a pair of glutamic acid residues in a conserved region of torsinA and appeared to have arisen independently in different ethnic populations.

paragraphs.text: In a man with late-onset oromandibular dystonia, Calakos et al. agent.process_note: I opened all 60 files. Only Calakos et al. (2010) had a full text, which I read in full. 43 papers were abstracts only and 16 were titles only. Of the title-only papers, I cited only Wooten 1973, Batshaw 1985 and Kamm 2008, and only for what their titles state. The others (the Zeman papers, Eldridge, Yanagisawa, Marsden, Ziegler, Wachtel, Motulsky, Zoossmann-Diskin, Ikeuchi) give no content to report. The papers identify the causal gene as DYT1/TOR1A (torsinA) on 9q34, with autosomal dominant inheritance and reduced penetrance. No HGNC reference data were supplied, so I gave no gene MIM number. The GAG deletion has no c. notation in these papers, so its HGVS entry follows the papers' wording (GAG deletion, Glu302/303del). Zygosity of the individual variants is not stated in the abstracts; heterozygosity rests on dominant inheritance and the haplotype data of Ozelius 1992. I did not cite Cheng 1996 (anticipation in adult-onset cranial/cervical dystonia) or the general reviews by Muller and Kupke 1990 and Nemeth 2002, because they do not address DYT1 specifically.
